name: Dakar
meta_description: TDSC investigative consulting in matters touching Dakar: port and trade counterparties, commercial court and arbitration support, and partner due diligence.
hero_lede: Dakar is Senegal's capital, main port and commercial centre, and a regional hub for West African finance, logistics and institutions. TDSC scopes investigative consulting from Nashville for matters touching the city, coordinating qualified Senegalese professionals and local counsel where local work is required.
intro: Dakar is the capital of Senegal and the centre of the Dakar Region, the country's smallest but most populous region, with 3,896,564 residents at the 2023 census. Government, banking, telecommunications, trade and services are concentrated on the Cape Verde peninsula, and the Port autonome de Dakar is one of West Africa's principal Atlantic ports. A study presented in July 2026 estimated that the port ecosystem handles about 24 million tonnes of goods a year and contributes 19 percent of Senegal's GDP. Growth is spreading east along the toll highway and regional express rail line to Diamniadio, a new administrative and industrial city near Blaise Diagne International Airport.

Organisations commission investigative work connected to Dakar because trade, infrastructure and public contracting converge there. Importers, freight forwarders and port concessionaires handle cargo for Senegal and landlocked neighbours such as Mali. Construction and infrastructure projects around Diamniadio and the airport draw foreign contractors and local partners. Senegal's oil and gas sector has added energy services, supply and joint venture activity. Lenders, investors and suppliers need to understand counterparties whose ownership and political connections are not always visible on the record, and disputes increasingly reach the Commercial Court of Dakar or arbitration in the city.

matters.title: Port, freight and customs counterparties
matters.text: Importers, forwarders, customs brokers and terminal operators in Dakar handle cargo for Senegal and transit to the interior. We research ownership, litigation and reputational history to identify front companies, undisclosed related parties and prior disputes before trade finance, agency or logistics contracts are signed.

matters.title: Transit trade to Mali
matters.text: Goods moving through Dakar to Mali and other inland markets pass through several intermediaries and jurisdictions. We trace the parties along the chain using RCCM extracts, court decisions and open sources, helping lenders, insurers and cargo interests investigate diversion, document irregularities or misdescribed shipments.

matters.title: Infrastructure and public contract partners
matters.text: Road, rail, airport and urban development projects around Dakar and Diamniadio involve public procurement and local partners. We examine partners' ownership, track record and links to politically exposed persons, supporting anti-corruption compliance and integrity reviews required by lenders and development finance institutions.

matters.title: Energy sector suppliers and joint ventures
matters.text: Senegal's oil and gas development has created demand for local suppliers, service companies and joint venture partners based in Dakar. We review ownership, beneficial ownership disclosures, local content claims and dispute history so that operators and investors understand who they are contracting with.

matters.title: Commercial disputes and asset research
matters.text: Creditors and claimants before the Commercial Court of Dakar or in arbitration need facts about counterparties, their assets and connected entities. We map businesses, property indicators and related parties from lawful sources so counsel can plan protective measures and enforcement under OHADA procedures.

local_context.title: Commercial Court of Dakar
local_context.text: The Tribunal de commerce hors classe de Dakar was created by Law No. 2017-24 of 28 June 2017 and installed in February 2018. It hears disputes between shareholders, banking and financial litigation, complex contract claims, enforcement of security interests and insolvency proceedings, with professional judges sitting alongside lay commercial judges from business. Law sets a three-month target for judgment after the first hearing, but a 2026 report noted understaffing and some cases lasting years.

local_context.title: Arbitration in Dakar
local_context.text: The Centre d'Arbitrage, de Médiation et de Conciliation de Dakar (CAMC-D), established in 1998 within the Dakar Chamber of Commerce, Industry and Agriculture, is Senegal's main arbitral institution and handles mainly domestic and West African regional cases. Arbitration is governed by the OHADA Uniform Act on Arbitration as revised in 2017. The Commercial Court of Dakar acts as supporting judge and enforcement judge for exequatur, with OHADA-related appeals ultimately to the CCJA in Abidjan.

local_context.title: Investment Code reform
local_context.text: Senegal replaced its 2004 Investment Code with Law No. 2025-16 of 27 September 2025. Under the new Article 51, investment disputes must first go through an amicable settlement process before recourse to the courts or to international arbitration under applicable treaties and agreements. Foreign investors with Dakar-based projects should review how the change affects dispute planning and the evidence they will need.

local_context.title: Diamniadio and the new city
local_context.text: Diamniadio, in Rufisque department about 30 km from central Dakar, is a planned new city intended to relieve population pressure on the capital. It houses ministries, a university and industrial areas, some of which have faced delays, and is linked to Dakar and Blaise Diagne International Airport by toll highway and the regional express train. Land allocation and construction contracts in this corridor are a recurring focus of diligence.

local_context.title: Regional and national bodies
local_context.text: Dakar hosts Senegal's national institutions and a number of regional and international organisations, and the national statistics agency (ANSD) publishes regional economic and social reports for Dakar. The Commercial Court registry holds most RCCM entries for the country. Practical access to many records still requires in-person searches, so research timelines are planned with local counsel. ANSD regional reports also provide useful context on Dakar's economy and employment.

tdsc_approach: TDSC has no office in Dakar and works on Dakar matters from Nashville. We agree the purpose with the client and its Senegalese counsel first, whether a port or trade counterparty review, a partner in an infrastructure or energy project, a dispute before the Commercial Court of Dakar or the CAMC-D, or an internal review, and scope the work to it. Sources include RCCM extracts and beneficial ownership information where accessible, court decisions, official gazettes, procurement notices and French-language media. Any registry searches, site visits or interviews in Dakar are carried out by qualified local professionals within Senegal's personal data law. Reports are prepared in English, with French translations of key documents where needed, and state sources and confidence.

faqs.q: Which court hears commercial disputes in Dakar?
faqs.a: The Tribunal de commerce hors classe de Dakar, created in 2017 and operating since 2018, hears shareholder, banking, contract, security enforcement and insolvency disputes, with professional and lay commercial judges. It can also order judicial mediation. Appeals go to the Court of Appeal, and on OHADA uniform law matters final review lies with the CCJA in Abidjan.

faqs.q: Can a dispute with a Dakar company be arbitrated locally?
faqs.a: Yes. The CAMC-D, attached to the Dakar Chamber of Commerce, administers domestic and regional arbitrations, and the OHADA Uniform Act on Arbitration provides the legal framework. Parties may also choose the CCJA's own arbitration or international institutions. The Commercial Court of Dakar supports proceedings and handles exequatur of awards.

faqs.q: How do you check a Dakar freight forwarder or importer?
faqs.a: We obtain RCCM information on registration, capital and managers, look for beneficial ownership data, and review court decisions, gazette notices and media in French and, where relevant, Wolof. We also look for related companies in Mali or other transit countries. Where records are not online, searches are carried out locally by qualified professionals.

faqs.q: Did Senegal's 2025 Investment Code change dispute options?
faqs.a: Law No. 2025-16 of 27 September 2025 replaced the 2004 code. Its Article 51 requires investment disputes to go first to an amicable settlement process, with recourse afterwards to the courts or to international arbitration under applicable treaties and agreements. Investors should take advice from Senegalese counsel on how this applies to their project.

faqs.q: Why do Diamniadio projects attract diligence?
faqs.a: Diamniadio is a government-led new city with ministries, industrial areas and infrastructure linked to the airport, and much of its development depends on land allocation and public contracts. Investors and lenders therefore look closely at partners' ownership, track record and political connections, and at whether land rights and permits are properly documented.

Port figures (24 million tonnes, 19 percent of GDP) come from a study presented by the port's staff association and reported by Le Soleil; they are not official statistics.

Stated from background knowledge, not verified in sources: Senegal's oil and gas development (kept generic), Mali transit trade, CFA franc, CAMC-D being attached to the Dakar Chamber of Commerce (supported by GAR search result title and country page, not opened), Wolof as a business language, presence of regional and international organisations in Dakar (kept generic).
